20.0.s.en: 1. The captivity of Egypt and Cush:

20.0.0.en: 1 In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it; 2 At the same time spake the LORD by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot. 3 And the LORD said, Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia; 4 So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.

20.0.1.en: Some critics thought that Sargon, king of Assyria, who sent Tartan to Ashdod, was Shalmaneser or Sennacherib. Others denied that a king of this name existed in Assyria; but, as Bultema says, God made the stones speak to put the unbelievers to shame, for it is known today that Sargon was one of the strongest kings of Assyria, and that he was the father of Sennacherib, having usurped the throne from Shalmaneser V and succeeded him.

20.0.2.en: The word "Sargon" means "appointed by God" or "the righteous king"; he used this name to cover over his usurping of the throne.

20.0.3.en: "Tartan" is not the name of a person, but most likely a title belonging to the command of the army.

20.0.4.en: Sargon sent the head of his army to Ashdod, aiming at Sua king of Egypt (2 Kgs 17:4), for Ashdod, which is on the border of the Philistines, was considered the key to entering Egypt.

20.0.5.en: Modern studies have revealed that Sua is not the name of a Pharaoh, but an abbreviation of the name of a commander of a battalion in the Delta called Siba, or an abbreviation of the name of a city in the western Delta called Sais, which Tefnakhte used as his residence.

20.0.6.en: Since Assyria had defeated Aram and Ephraim, the time had come to strike Pharaoh; so the king sent his commander to Ashdod and he conquered it, the same commander whom Sennacherib used in the siege of Jerusalem.

20.1.0.en: God wished to move the feelings of His people, change their hearts and rebuke them for their reliance on Egypt and Cush; therefore He asked His prophet to walk before the people naked and barefoot for three years, to be himself a prophecy of what would befall Egypt and Cush when Assyria would take them captive and lead their great men into captivity as slaves, naked, barefoot and with their buttocks uncovered... Isaiah himself became a sign and wonder [3], mocked by all who looked at him because of what had come upon him, and this for the salvation of his people and to keep them from relying on Pharaoh of Egypt.

20.1.1.en: Isaiah, in his sufferings and nakedness, bore a shadow of the sufferings of the Lord Christ, who endured nakedness in order to clothe us with His righteousness, and bore the wounds of His people in His body in order to heal us. Isaiah walked as a slave, wearing no outer garment and no sandals, a picture of his Lord who became as a slave (Phil 2:7) in order to free us from the yoke of bondage.

20.2.0.en: 5 And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory. 6 And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day, Behold, such is our refuge, whither we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?

20.3.0.en: When Pharaoh of Egypt submits to Assyria, the children of Judah are terrified, their hope is shattered, and Egypt, their glory, is humbled, and they say: "Behold, such is our refuge, whither we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?" [6].

20.3.1.en: This is the end of everyone who relies on an arm of flesh!

21.0.0.en: 1 The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds in the south pass through; so it cometh from the desert, from a terrible land. 2 A grievous vision is declared unto me; the plunderer plundering, and the destroyer destroying. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease. 3 Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it. 4 My heart wandered, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into trembling unto me. 5 They prepare the table, they watch in the watchtower, they eat, they drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield. 6 For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth. 7 And he saw riders, couples of horsemen, riders of asses, riders of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed: 8 And he cried like a lion: My lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower in the daytime, and I am set in my ward whole nights: 9 And, behold, here are riders of men, couples of horsemen. And he answered and said, Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground. 10 O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you.

21.0.1.en: The prophet Isaiah refers to Babylon by a strange symbolic name: "The burden of the desert of the sea" [1]. He called Babylon, the golden city, the glory of the nations, a desert because of its evil, which turned it into a state of wasteland; and it was called "the desert of the sea" because of its location on the river Euphrates, or because it was the capital of more than one nation among the nations, for waters signify the many peoples, so that it became a dry desert in the midst of the peoples.

21.0.2.en: The Jews believe that the demons dwell in three regions of the world: the barren deserts, the waters, and the air; therefore the Lord Christ fought the devil during His temptation on the mountain in the wilderness and overcame, and fought him in the waters of the Jordan as in his lair and overcame, and also fought him in the air when He was lifted up on the Cross and triumphed. Babylon was called "the desert of the sea" to affirm that it became the place of Satan, who dwells in the desert and also in the sea. St. John the Theologian saw it as a harlot woman sitting upon many waters (Rev 17:1).

21.0.3.en: The prophet Isaiah saw the army of Cyrus, coming to carry out the plan of God concerning Babylon, like whirlwinds in the south, like a storm coming from the desert, from a terrible land [1].

21.0.4.en: The whirlwinds or violent winds in the south mean that they are hot, as opposed to those coming from the north, which are cold; as though the army of Cyrus were like hot, violent winds accompanied by a storm from the desert laden with sand, which buries the fields, spoils the crops, damages the houses and roads, and causes diseases, especially of the eyes. In other words, it shatters man's resources, his dwelling and his insight. This is contrary to the hot but gentle southern winds, which cause the crops to ripen; for this reason the bride says: "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 4:16).

21.1.0.en: The prophet, in his wonderful tenderness even toward enemies, could not bear to see the ruin and plunder that came upon Babylon [2], and so he says: "Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it. My heart wandered, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into trembling unto me" [3-4].

21.2.0.en: It appears that he saw this vision at night [4], for the night of his delight in prayer was turned into trembling... And perhaps he speaks here in the name of the Babylonians, for whom the night of feasting and joy turned into trembling because of Cyrus' storming of the capital; for he saw the royal table prepared and the guards amusing themselves with eating and drinking, though it was fitting for the princes to anoint the shield with oil in order to fight Cyrus.

21.2.1.en: The prophet could not bear to see Babylon with its great men amusing themselves without concern while the enemy stormed the gates that had become unguarded, so the prophet's heart wandered and was filled with terror and pain. I say, how should we also not groan for the servants who are occupied away from the spiritual struggle with formalities, official matters and feasts, leaving the Church of God and its flock as though without a watchful guard.

21.2.2.en: The words of St. John Chrysostom concerning pastoral care remain immortal.

21.2.3.en: [I am a father full of compassion. Hear what Paul asks: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth" (Gal 4:19). Every mother cries out as she travails in the hour of birth; so do I also].

21.2.4.en: [I wish you could see the fires burning in my heart, that you might know that I burn more than a young woman groaning over her early widowhood; for I do not think she grieves over her husband, nor does a father grieve over his son, as I grieve over this crowd gathered here]...

21.3.0.en: The divine call came to the prophet: "Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth" [6], for in ancient times the prophet was called a "watchman" or "sentinel," as he was called a "seer." The work of the prophet is to watch from the high tower and guard souls with the word of God, as well as to see with spiritual insight in order to declare the will of God and His plan of salvation.

21.3.1.en: The prophet Habakkuk stood as a sentinel, for he says: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me" (Hab 2:1); and the prophet Ezekiel was called a sentinel in more than one place (Ezek 3:17; 33:2, 6, 7).

21.4.0.en: Isaiah saw Persia (riders of asses) and Media (riders of camels) coming to seize Babylon; he saw and heard with great attention [7], for the matter is serious and grave, touching the life of his people. He did not stop at seeing and listening, but began to roar like a lion [8] to declare the plan of God for the fall of Babylon and the salvation of the people of God.

21.5.0.en: "Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground. O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you" [9-10].

21.5.1.en: The repetition of an expression twice, such as "Babylon is fallen, is fallen," is one of the features of this book (Isa 21:9; 24:4, 16; 28:13; 29:1; 40:1, 9; 43:11; etc.), perhaps because the speech in this book of salvation is addressed to the Gentiles as well as to the Jews, the call to salvation being universal, to accept the God of all and to overcome evil. It is fitting here for every person - whether of Gentile or Jewish origin - to be assured that Babylon, which captured his heart with lusts and gave him violence, collapses before the salvation of God, so that the heavenly Jerusalem may arise in his heart. Let all the idols of Babylon collapse, that the Lord may arise in the heart and declare His Kingdom. Moreover the repetition also means a kind of emphasis. Besides that, the repetition of two carries a symbol of the love that makes the two one, as St. Augustine says. By love the inner Babylon falls and the kingdom of the devil, who cannot bear love, collapses, and through it we enjoy the evangelical life according to the Lord's commandment: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (Jn 13:35).

21.5.2.en: The prophet sees the world as a threshing floor, on which the crops are trodden and then winnowed to separate the wheat hidden among the straw... It is the wheat of the Lord Himself, which does not perish but is separated from the chaff.

21.5.3.en: St. Augustine speaks of the Babylonian captivity and the deliverance from it, saying:

21.5.4.en: [The Apostle says: "Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come" (1 Cor 10:1). We must know our captivity, and then our deliverance; it is fitting for us to know Babylon in which we were taken captive, and Jerusalem to which we groan to return. For these two cities - as to the letter - are two actual cities.

21.5.6.en: These two cities were built at a particular time to be a symbol of two cities that remain until the end of the world... when some sit on the right and the others on the left, Jerusalem will be on the right and Babylon on the left...

21.5.7.en: Two kinds of love found these two cities: the love of God founds Jerusalem, and the love of the world founds Babylon. Therefore let each one ask himself: what is it that he loves? And then he will know which city is his homeland. If he finds Babylon to be his homeland, let him uproot covetousness from himself and plant love; but if he finds Jerusalem to be his homeland, let him endure the captivity, hoping for freedom...

21.5.8.en: Now, brethren, may we hear about this city of which we are citizens; may we hear about it and sing of it and long for it].

21.5.9.en: Thus St. Augustine looks to the children of God who are bound by divine love as citizens of the Jerusalem above, the city of eternal love; they live here in struggle against Babylon, which does not cease to spend all its energies to take the children of God captive and deprive them of their heavenly homeland, since they themselves delivered themselves up to captivity when they accepted sin; and the Savior has come to open the door of hope to them, to grant them the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

21.5.10.en: In a look full of hope St. Augustine comments on the saying of the prophet: "When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted" (Ps 126:1), saying: [Man was a citizen of Jerusalem, but he was sold under sin and became a wanderer (without a city)...

21.5.11.en: "Babylon" means "confusion"... for the affairs of this present human life are all confusion, as they do not belong to God. In the midst of this confusion, in this Babylonian land, Zion was taken captive, but "the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion," so that we became "like those who are comforted," that is, we rejoiced because we received comfort...

21.5.12.en: We grieve over what we are now, but we are comforted in hope. The present, which is for our grief, will pass, and eternal joy will come, and there will be no need of comfort where we are not afflicted with any tribulation].

21.6.0.en: "The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come" [11-12].

21.6.1.en: The prophet calls Adam by a secret prophetic name, "Dumah," which is an abbreviation of Idumea. If the name "Edom" means "bloody" or "earthy," since Edom represents the wicked who love shedding blood, bound to the love of earthly, temporal and fleshly things, then the name "Dumah" means "silence" or "the silence of death"...

21.6.2.en: The prophet stood on the watchtower all the nights [8], for a kind of inner darkness reigned over the world, awaiting the coming of the Sun of Righteousness to remove the darkness of the night and for the morning to come. Now he hears a voice, perhaps from heaven or from the rest of the prophets and men of God: "Watchman, what of the night?"... The fullness of time has come and the light of morning has dawned; let the nations be silent and die to their old man to enjoy the light of life; let them seek now and find their light through their faith in the Lord Christ, let them return to God their Savior and come to Him, and find Him stretching out His hands with practical love to embrace them.

21.6.3.en: "Watchman, what of the night?" is repeated twice because the speech with the prophet concerns the Jews as well as the Gentiles, and also the believers of the Old and New Testaments, that all may enjoy salvation while they are in stillness contemplating the work of God with them.

21.7.0.en: 13 The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim. 14 Bring water to meet the thirsty, O inhabitants of the land of Tema, meet the fugitive with his bread. 15 For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war. 16 For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Within a year, according to the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail: 17 And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished: for the LORD God of Israel hath spoken it.

21.7.1.en: The original reads Ereb and not Arabia, which means "evening," for it speaks of all who dwell in darkness.

21.7.2.en: Here he addresses the tribes of Dedan and Kedar, who dwell southeast of Edom; these received those fleeing from the sword, who gave themselves up in return for enjoying water to drink or bread to eat..

21.7.3.en: Since these tribes lived in the darkness of paganism, they became unable to offer real help to those who fled to them, because a blind man leading a blind man, both fall into a ditch (Mt 15:14; Lk 6:39).
